title: I made a card-slapping game in 4 days with a pile of AI agents. Writing the code was the easy part.
author: Marmzzzzzz
selftext:
Solo entry for the Epic AI MegaJam. Back in August I shelved an idea for a card game, the theme turned out to be "Director's Cut", so I took it off the shelf. You hold a card, swing the mouse and slam it on the table, in a tournament against alien rivals inside a toy shop on a space station. There's also air hockey, ping pong and a VR mode.



My setup: Claude Code as the main orchestrator, Codex (GPT-6 Astra) for a lot of the C++ and code review, Hermes on the side, spread across four PCs at home. Unreal 5.9, mostly C++. Meshy for 3D models, ElevenLabs for sound effects, Blender driven by agents for the station itself.



Some things I didn't expect:



The agents were rarely the bottleneck, the builds were. At one point I measured it and about 85% of the time on test runs went to waiting in the build queue. Adding more agents just made the queue longer.



Letting several agents edit the same core files was a mess. My player and HUD files went through 11 different writers in one day and every merge conflicted. What fixed it: new features go into new .cpp files, the core only gets a one-line call, and only one agent is allowed inside the core at a time.



"Works in the editor" means nothing. In an early package, DLSS ran fine in editor runs but silently never loaded, because the plugin was marked "Optional" in the .uproject. The console variables were still there, so it looked like it was working. It was a one-line fix, but since then nothing counts as done until I see it in the packaged game's log.



Never let an agent make a whole set before you approve one sample. I asked for cards and got 95 of them back that looked like app icons.



"Make it feel better" gets you nowhere. Once I started talking about grip, release velocity and what a short click should do, the fixes actually landed.



Music was my favourite part, mostly because the agents are deaf. I picked a reference track for the mood, and a script measured it and every one of our renders the same way: tempo, key, loudness every 4 seconds across six frequency bands, stereo width, hits per second, how hard the sidechain pumps, plus waveform and spectrogram images. So the agents "listened" by comparing tables and pictures. On version 10, for example, the numbers showed the track climbing from about -19 dB in the intro to -14 dB at the finale, which was the shape I wanted. But a second agent reading the spectrograms flagged the lead synth as buzzy. It tested the lead's distortion on its own, found a third harmonic only 21 dB below the note, and softened it. It also caught a stereo widening trick that made the mix wobble by up to 3.6 dB when played in mono. The notes were all ours, rendered in Python with Ableton's Core Library samples; the reference was only there for feel. Then I'd listen and say yes or no. Strangely human loop.



Curious how others deal with this: how do you stop multiple agents from stepping on the same files? And has anyone found a decent way to let agents judge feel or visuals without a human playing every single build?
